messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya is an 18-year-old architect of Middle Eastern descent, single, and living alone in a quiet apartment complex. The traumatic event occurred six months ago, when she was walking home from her office late one evening. As she turned onto her street, she witnessed a man being violently attacked by a group of individuals outside a convenience store. He was struck repeatedly, and Maya froze, unable to move or call for help, until the attackers fled and the man lay bleeding on the pavement. She remembers the sound of his cries and the sight of blood pooling under his head as though it were happening again in that moment. Since that night, Maya has struggled to feel safe.

In the weeks following the incident, Maya found herself unable to shake the images and sounds that replayed in her mind without warning. She began to avoid walking that route home, taking a longer, unfamiliar path that added twenty minutes to her commute. At work, where she designs residential buildings, she found herself scanning the windows of her office for any sign of movement outside, her heart racing whenever a car backfired or a door slammed in the hallway. She had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that violence could erupt at any moment, and that she was powerless to prevent it. This belief colored everything: she stopped going out after dark, declined invitations from colleagues to grab dinner, and began sleeping poorly.

Maya’s difficulty falling asleep stems from a need to stay alert. Each night, as she lies in bed, she listens for footsteps in the hallway or the creak of a door, certain that if she lets her guard down, something terrible will happen. This hypervigilance has left her exhausted, and she often wakes feeling as though she has not rested at all. During the day, she is superalert, constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats. She notices every person who walks too close to her on the sidewalk, every car that slows down near her, every shadow that moves in her peripheral vision. She has strong negative feelings—fear, horror, anger at the attackers, guilt for not intervening, and shame for her paralysis—that surge up unpredictably, often when she sees a crowd or hears raised voices.

These feelings are intense and overwhelming, but they do not seem to be connected to any particular thought or memory in a way that Maya can trace. She simply finds herself flooded with dread or rage, sometimes for no apparent reason. At work, she has become withdrawn, avoiding the open-plan office’s communal areas because the noise and movement feel threatening. Her supervisor has noticed her reduced productivity and asked if she is okay, but Maya brushed it off, unwilling to explain. She has started to believe that others can see her fear, that they think she is weak or broken, and this has made her avoid social interactions even more.

What finally brought Maya to seek help was a moment last week when she was designing a new building’s entrance. She looked at the blueprint and saw the glass doors, the open lobby, and felt a surge of panic so strong she had to leave the room. She realized she could not picture herself walking through that entrance without imagining an attack. That night, she could not sleep at all, and the next morning she called a therapist. She is most afraid that this fear will never go away, that she will be trapped in this state of constant alertness forever, unable to live the life she had planned. She hopes, quietly, that someone can help her feel safe again.
